utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, ma'am. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So good morning, everybody. I see the -- if there are problems with interpretation, as usual let me know, please. All right. Mr. Bourgon, who is missing. Mr. Haynes, yesterday I noticed you had a new member on your team that I had not noticed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of our legal assistants. That's Ingrid Morgan. Sorry, I didn't introduce her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's just the way I'm intervening --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: By the way, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Madam Fauveau, is your team here?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Prosecution, I don't -- I see Mr. Nicholls. I also thought for a moment that I saw Mr. Van der Puye. So it's Mr. Nicholls and Mr. McCloskey. I am informed that there are some preliminaries. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just this at the end of the session yesterday Mr. Ostojic pointed out that the witness had a notepad in front of him that had some handwriting on it, and I asked if I can inquire about. I asked the court usher this morning if she would ask the witness if Mr. Ostojic could take a look at those notes. And I guess he agreed because they were brought out and I think a copy has been made for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to go into it as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know if they have a copy. They requested a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We would not preempt the issue because we've heard you. We haven't heard Mr. Ostojic and we haven't heard the witness. So if there is a problem, objection on the part of the witness, or on your part, I don't know, then we'll deal with the matter, but otherwise please --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So anything else? None? Madam Usher, could you kindly bring the witness in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome once more. Mr. Nicholls will be finishing his direct within the next hour or so, and then we start with the cross-examinations. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. Just a few more topics I wish to cover with you this morning. When we left off yesterday, we were talking about the 12th of July, after the third meeting at the Hotel Fontana. You described how you went to Potocari after that meeting and then returned to Bratunac in order to talk to Momir Nikolic, and then you returned from Bratunac again to Potocari. And what I'd like to ask you about now is if you could please describe the scene at Potocari on 12th of July after you returned from Bratunac for the last time when you had tried to speak to Momir Nikolic. What did you see there? What was going on?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drove back in my own Mercedes. The intention was to return to the compound. At Potocari I saw lines of buses and trucks heading toward Potocari. I overtook them. Some of the buses and trucks had already passed our camp, and at the entrance to our camp or slightly beyond that you could see VRS soldiers present, including General Mladic. They were speaking with the population, that is to say the refugees, and appeared to be planning to prepare transport and board the people. A camera crew was there as well. It was a Serb camera crew to record what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why do you say they appeared to be planning to transport and board people? How did you arrive at that impression?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was driving without an interpreter because our own Muslim interpreter was too frightened to head toward Bratunac. The only interpreter who was not afraid was my interpreter Petar, and he wasn't available. So I tried to follow what was happening, but I couldn't always understand everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was, as far as you could see, what was the Muslim population doing at this point while -- while the VRS were there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire area had been closed off with red tape. There were a few DutchBat soldiers present as well. The population was waiting. Some were curious about what would happen and looked like they were interested in making a run. That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you personally speak to or attempt to speak to Mladic while you were in Potocari at this time?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried. Upon arriving, when I saw what was happening, I went to the camp and addressed Lieutenant Colonel Karremans at the command post and mentioned what was happening in my view. Lieutenant Colonel Karremans requested that I approach Mladic and at the very least object to him. I was to point out to him that the infirmed, the elderly, and the women should be transported first. So with that in mind, I headed off in that direction, and if I remember correctly an interpreter was with me, or at least Petar was there. At least somebody to speak with. I headed toward General Mladic. At that moment or slightly afterwards, somebody from MSF, Medecins sans Frontieres, joined us and the three of us started talking, and later on Lieutenant Colonel Karremans joined us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you able to make your objection to Mladic, and what happened?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: He listened to our objections, but nothing happened as a result because the buses and trucks, later on the trucks, were indeed filled with people who were waiting there without any selection of the injured or the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you able yourself personally to see people being putting on these buses?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that personally. I walked past the buses to see what was happening. At first the arrangement was that at least one or two DutchBat soldiers would accompany each bus, but that didn't work out. I assume it was the rush that everything happened with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what people were being put on the buses, men, women, children? Can you just describe the people you saw who boarded onto the buses?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the first convoy that departed. What I saw consisted largely of elderly women, children, and in some cases some boys and here and there a considerable number of elderly men and a few individual men between the ages of 16 and 60, but most were elderly women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a very short video clip now that's number 2009. If you could look at your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you able to see and hear the video clip, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I caught the point when it started. I know that it finished at 1.58 something, but anyway, the video started at 1 hour, 57 minutes, 28 seconds, and finished at about one minute later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we can have the last still, we can put it on record with more precision. And I would prefer it that way, because it's -- no, no. It's right to the end. That's it. 1:58:50. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to make -- this is, I take it, part of one much longer video recording, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. It's part of the entire -- what we call the trial video, but this segment has an individual 65 ter number for the record, although it is an extract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So -- but it's -- as such, what we have seen is the entire segment of 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps as we go along and we make use of further videos, if there are segments you could kindly tell us that they are segments and whether it's the entire segment that we're seeing or whether it's only part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. It's just to streamline the procedure and make it a uniform one as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I will say for the record that all of the clips I played yesterday were entire clips. There were no excerpts from clips, and I think I gave the 65 ter number for all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, you did, and in fact I made a record of that. Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the part of at that clip that I'm interested in, Colonel, is where General Mladic speaks to the person speaking initially with the blue helmet, the DutchBat officer, who says to General Mladic: "Roger. I will inform our commander. Our commander has no information about a plan." General Mladic in response: "It regards my order. I couldn't care less for your commander. We will board everyone who wants it." Can you just comment on that answer from General Mladic and how it fits into what you've been saying about the concerns you had with the boarding process?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, General Mladic did what he said. This happened without consulting DutchBat, or at any rate, without considering the arrangement that DutchBat felt it had made with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You talked about the convoy that you saw. There were a few men on it, mostly women, children, and the elderly. Did you see what was happening to the men between 16 and 60 in Potocari while you were there? Still speaking about the 12th of July, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was a building across from Potocari where men of Muslim descent were gathered. The building was guarded by VRS soldiers. I saw it happening. I entered the building briefly. I was in the first room on the ground floor, and I saw some Muslim prisoners sitting on the floor. There were some passports in a corner, or other identity cards. I wanted to continue looking around the building, but I didn't have authorisation, and I was removed from the building. And I received a clear indication with a gun that I should leave or I would run into problems. And around the back of that same building I saw, in any case, a group of VRS soldiers marching off behind the building to do something that was not clear to me. These soldiers were being marched off by Mladic's bodyguard who recognised me and said, "Pay attention to what we're doing." I couldn't accompany them. I was stopped by some dogs. And later on I heard shots being fired behind the building. And those are my observations about what was happening with the Muslim men at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, before we go on, in the answer to the previous question, Colonel Boering had said that, "In my view" -- it's page 7, line 10. "In my view, General Mladic did what he said." I wonder if the witness could clarify what Mladic had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, please, Colonel. If you could explain what you meant by that part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quoting what General Mladic indicated on the video, which was that he was not concerned about what Lieutenant Colonel Karremans was saying, that he would do what he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that he did do what he wanted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is: Which is what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was it that he wanted to do? If you can explain that that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to look in somebody else's mind, but I assumed that he had the intention to transport refugees by buses in the way he wanted it to happen, without any consultation or without any difficult selection procedures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's still not clear to me, but I believe it will be further explored during the cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you it this way, still on the same topic, Colonel: What Mladic said was, "I couldn't care less for your commander. We'll board everybody who wants it." And you answered, "In my view, General Mladic did what he said," and you've explained that you thought that General Mladic didn't care or consider any arrangement that had been made with DutchBat. Did you mean any more than that, or anything else you can add to -- to your comment that General Mladic did what he said he was going to do?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: A discussion was going on with a representative of MSF, who insisted that we should care for the wounded, that they should be transported in a fitting manner, and General Mladic was extremely short in the way he communicated with the MSF representatives. He indicated that the person in question was not a military personnel and that the operation had to be executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me go back to the question you -- we were talking about, your last answer about the house where the men were gathered, the Muslim men. Who was gathering the men into this house? How were they gathered, as you say, into this building?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were gathered by VRS soldiers. As to how they were gathered, I can say that from among the population gathered near the compound for as far as I could see, men were selected and subsequently led towards the building. During the short moment that I could observe people travelling off by bus, I could also see moments where people were not allowed into the buses and had to step aside and were subsequently led off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you're referring there to men who were not allowed to board?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen this in the case of one man at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the other event you described was, if I understood you correctly, bodyguards for Mladic marching somebody behind the White House and telling you --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that. He hasn't given any evidence as to it being a White House.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained. In fact, one of the things I wanted you to address was this building because there were several buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Marching somebody behind the building and telling you to pay attention, and you said that the person -- that there was a soldier being marched behind the building. Who was being marched behind the building by Mladic's bodyguards? Can you explain that a bit more?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant to say that the bodyguard of Mladic gathered -- had gathered a number of VRS soldiers, that he led them behind the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened then was that we heard shots being fired behind the building. And my attempts to try and take a look at what was going on behind, this was prevented by VRS soldiers who had dogs. So therefore, I could not take a look at the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So this bodyguard of Mladic gathered some VRS soldiers and led them behind the building. Did anybody else go behind the building with the soldiers and Mladic's bodyguard? Did they bring anybody with them?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And as best you can recall, what exactly did the bodyguard say to you when he addressed you? Try to remember.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said to me in English, "Look, Major, what I'm going to do."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you an image now. It's number 1535.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On what ground?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, the witness hasn't given a description of the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, this may well be an issue, Your Honour, in terms of which building it is that he's talking about and I'd ask him to give a description first before being shown the photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry to disappoint you, Ms. Condon, but we don't see the -- any validity in your objection. So, Mr. Nicholls, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Colonel, can you take a look at that picture and tell me if you recognise the building in the picture or any of the buildings in the picture.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can recognise this building as the so-called white building or White House. The building behind it, behind the electricity poles a little bit to the left, is also a building I remember. This is a former factory, and this very clearly is the building I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be very clear, could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I mean, we need to be clear. Which -- this is confusing. He's -- first he refers to one building which he maintains is the so-called White House. Then he refers to the other building with which he seems to be familiar, too, describing it as a former factory, and then immediately after he said, "And this is very clearly the building I was referring to." Which of the two buildings was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was going to ask that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you could maybe take the pen, Colonel, or the stylus, and please mark the building which you've called the former factory. Just draw --

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. This, what I'm pointing at now, is the former factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Colonel. We'll get it working in a minute.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet. I can give some short comments. We see the white building. We see the high tension electric wires. We see a white building to the right of the electricity poles which is the white building I referred to, which is the building in which the prisoners were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm glad I'm in a courtroom, not in a dentist's clinic. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, he can't mark the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay. I think we have understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So I'd ask the record to reflect that he has identified the white building at the right of the photo, to the right of the electrical pylons is the building he was describing is where the prisoners were held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think his description was enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you went into the building and you saw the prisoners there, could you tell me approximately how many prisoners you saw, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 8 or 10. Eight to ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you say you saw some passports or identity cards. How were you able to tell what those were? Or how did you decide that those documents were passports or identity cards?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had been in the enclave from January to June. Regularly we would deal with people who would apply for jobs for DutchBat or people who needed to be transported because they were wounded towards Tuzla. So in those cases we dealt with ID cards. We had to establish the identity of people. This was part of my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you do anything after -- after you had been told to leave this building where the prisoners were held, the White House? What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went outside. There I saw a United Nations observer. I believe it has been Major Kingori from Africa, who was there together with the Dutch United Nations observers, Mr. De Haan. I asked them to keep surveilling the building or at least count the number of people that would enter it from that point in order to keep an overview of the situation, and they indicated that they would do this. Subsequently, I left in order to continue my inspection of events in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you say you asked them to keep count of the number of people that would enter the building, do you mean keep count of the number of VRS soldiers or keep count of the number of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the number of prisoners or people taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about how you came to leave Potocari that day and about the first convoy. If you describe what you did after -- after leaving the -- after the events you've just described.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That moment the buses and trucks were loaded with refugees. It was unclear where the buses and the trucks with the refugees would travel to. Near the entrance to the camp, Major Franken was present, the deputy commander of DutchBat, and he asked me to accompany the first convoy with my Mercedes in order to see what was going on. And he also presented another person, Major Voerman, and both of us were to accompany or to follow the convoy. Subsequently, I quickly gathered some belongings. I took the car and we drove up to the head of the column. And at that moment the column was already departing, so I caught up with the column and I checked where they were driving to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The transcript didn't catch the name of the other major who accompanied the column. Could you give us that name again?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of the other person was a captain, not major, Captain Voerman, V-O-E-R-M-A-N.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. How many buses were in this convoy? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe 10. There also was a number of trucks, approximately six.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was there any VRS escort for the convoy?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first vehicle was a civilian vehicle where the major I referred to before, the person responsible for the transport of the refugees was present, and this vehicle drove at the head and the man inside was the somewhat organiser of the general events. Near the sides of the road, near crossroads that we passed, we also saw VRS soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That VRS officer you're referring to, is that the person you called Kosavic or Kozaric earlier?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would like you to look at map 5?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is he sure of his rank, that was a major or not something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you remember the rank, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot state this with certainty. I believed him to have been a major, but here my memory is not completely certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you describe -- can you describe, while we are getting the map, the route the convoy took?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I use a pen or simply tell you orally?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You can just tell us orally as we look along with you on the map?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Potocari to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Take a moment to look at the map, sir.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then at Bratunac, left at Bratunac, and then it continued to Glogova, Kravica, Sandici, to the left toward Milici, and that takes you to the junction at Maglici, to the right at Vlasenica and then ending up at Tisca. That's the route we travelled. Later on the route was clear to me, but at the time I didn't have a map with me, and I simply followed to see where we were going. At the point I knew Bratunac, but the other places we drove to at a certain point I saw a sign saying Milici and the name of Vlasenica. I saw that as well. I didn't have a map with me, but I'm positive this is the route we drove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question, Colonel. While you lived there in Srebrenica, did you familiarise yourself with the Cyrillic alphabet and script?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I studied Greek and Latin, so I had some familiarity with those languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the purpose of my question was to get to know from you whether you would have encountered at the time any difficulties in identifying signs along the road.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I could recognise them and figure them out. It wasn't easy, but I could do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that information. Mr. Nicholls, he's back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, at any point were any passengers or people who were on that convoy taken off and separated from the convoy?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember is that the convoy generally continued along the same direction. On the road between Bratunac and Milici, we made one stop because of a shooting that took place. Then we continued through Milici and somewhere near Tisca we stopped. There the people were de-boarded from the buses and trucks. They were assembled, and at that point I saw that some men were selected and taken away separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many men, approximately, were selected and taken away separately?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my observations, perhaps 10 or 15. I didn't see any more there. It was very crowded there, and I didn't have much freedom of movement left any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What were the ages of these men who you saw being separated?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say they were older than about 14 and younger -- it's difficult to estimate. 60 or 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you see where these men were taken or what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were separated in the direction of the forest. I tried to see where they were going, but at a certain point I was blocked and taken back to our position where most of the refugees were. I was not authorised to walk any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. A couple questions. Who separated the men and took them off, and who was it who blocked you? If you could answer those two questions separately.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near Tisca they were VRS soldiers, and the person in charge who I remembered from a previous meeting was Major Sarkic. He was the organiser, and he indicated that he was doing this job upon assignment from the Drina Corps, with his militia brigade. He mentioned that in broken German.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it says militia brigade, but can you tell us if you remember which brigade Sarkic was attached to?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, he was an LO with the militia [as interpreted] brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think you said "Milici". It's been translated as "militia".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, just to be sure we're not confusing it with the town Milici. Perhaps somebody who is perhaps following in B/C/S would get confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: LO being liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is that correct, Colonel, that Sarkic was the liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was introduced as a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you ask him any questions about what was happening with these men and where they were going? You already described what he said, but was there any other discussion with him? And by "these men," I'm sorry, I mean the prisoners who were led off.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I do remember that I was surprised that I wasn't allowed any further to see what was happening, and I was going to report this as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How were you able to communicate with Major Sarkic? Did you have an interpreter, or how were you able to speak with him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he already said that they conversed in broken German -- or, rather, that Sarkic spoke broken German.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm sure you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a short video now. It's 2037. And if -- this will be the entire clip. It is extract from the larger trial video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's kind of blurry, but can you see yourself in this picture anywhere? If not, we can play it some more. And we're at 2:15:28.8.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see myself in the upper-left corner next to the soldier, and there's a small boy in front of me with a white shirt. I'm next to the soldier with the belt. And on my left it's difficult to see. There's Captain Voerman also from DutchBat. He's wearing a blue beret or helmet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could play the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Colonel, could you -- you were there. Can you describe what we've just seen in this video. What's going on there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the end of a walk through no man's land. Between the two fronts was a road that had not been used for a long time. I think they walked about five or six metres [as interpreted] across it, and at the other end they continued on toward Kladanj and that brought them to the Muslim side. And then you see -- part of the video you see the reception there. It was quite hot, and the transportation went from the enclave to Tisca, and after waiting -- the walking and waiting took a few hours, and especially by the end, quite a few people were at the end of their rope, and they were thirsty and hungry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why did you walk with these people we've seen on the video, the people from the convoy, over into the Muslim-held territory?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was requested by Major Sarkic. When I arrived, he was working with VRS soldiers to de-mine the area where they would be walking. He was uncertain of part of the route. He was afraid of coming too close to an area with Muslim fighters. So that's why he urgently requested me and Captain Voerman to escort the first group as liaisons so that the refugees would be confident they were heading in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 20, line 2 of the transcript, it said that this walk from Tisca to Kladanj was five or six metres. Is that supposed to be kilometres?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe it was five kilometres. It wasn't metres. Four or five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nicholls, it's still not clear to me whether in his testimony the witness, Colonel Boering, meant to tell us that Colonel Sarkic or Major Sarkic had left with the convoy from Potocari or whether just found him there when they stopped near Tisca. If he could explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel, please. Was Major Sarkic -- did he accompany the convoy from Potocari, or did you meet him in Tisca when the people were taken off the buses?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him in Tisca. He was a bit taken aback by the large number of refugees arriving and asked me whether I could tell him how many refugees were coming and how many needed to be processed, because he wasn't equipped for that. So Major Sarkic was not if full communication with Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Finally, I want to ask you - I'm coming to the end of my questions - what you did after reaching Kladanj. Were you able to contact your command? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I was taken prisoner, in a manner of speaking, by Muslim soldiers who wanted to start by interrogating me about who I was. They didn't trust me. It took some time. And then we were fetched, I don't remember exactly who it was, by a UN soldier, and then we were taken ahead by a Dutch soldiers who took us to a Dutch group in the neighbourhood. I made my reports, and after consulting the battalion on Lieutenant Colonel Karremans, we did not return, and from there I returned home via Split. I spent about a week there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We've finally arrived at the cross-examination. Have you -- are you going to continue using the same pattern as before? Will you go first, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The order is the same but cross-examination of this witness will be by Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, I'd like to ask you some questions about your role as liaison officer. Yes? You've given evidence about the fact that you maintained contact with the civilian leadership at Srebrenica. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And you've given evidence in relation to your contacts with the leaders in the 28th Division of the ABiH; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the role of a liaison officer is an information-gathering exercise? Is that a fair description?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the commander also gives you authorisation up to a certain level, and beyond that he has to act in that interim area you act on behalf of the commander. So it's more than simply gathering information. You also have a mandate, but that grows through your understanding with the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's right, isn't it? You reported directly to Lieutenant Colonel Karremans, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. So in those meetings that you would have on a weekly basis with, for example, the leaders of the 28th Division, you would no doubt report back that -- back to Lieutenant Colonel Karremans as to the outcome of those meetings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in preparing for the meetings, as well if incidents occurred, you would review those and discuss them. And if there were major incidents, then you would come along, or Major Franken would come along.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps if I can put it to you in a more overt way. Would you consider yourself in the same capacity as an intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those are different, two different things, an intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But you agree that your role was, as we discussed, to obtain information from the meetings that you attended. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Condon, he's confirmed already that that was part of his overall function but couldn't constitute the beginning and the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you in relation to your meetings with the military leadership of the 28th Division, where were those meetings held, Colonel Boering?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most occurred in the postal building where the UN representatives were present, and very occasionally they were convened at the camp in Potocari or in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: When you refer to the postal buildings, I think you made a reference to that as the PTT building in one of your statements. Is that the same building that you're referring to? Yes. I see you nodding.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Is that also as you understood it the building that was used as the quasi-headquarters of the 28th Division at that time, or one of the buildings?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was used as headquarters but not the headquarters of 28th Division. Occasionally meetings were convened there, but it was used primarily for using the connections with Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Condon. Sorry to interrupt you, but I think lines 24 and 25 of page 23 and first line of page 24 need some clarification, because as it is it would convey the idea that the PTT building that he's referring to is not the PTT building in Srebrenica. You're referring to the PTT building in Srebrenica, which is in front of the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's correct. It's near the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, just so we're clear, when you say it was used as headquarters, what do you exactly mean by that, Colonel Boering?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say it was intended as a headquarters. I said that it could be used as a place to establish connections and to contact Tuzla from there. Meetings with the local population, such as the mayor, they were held in the town hall, and that was with the ABiH soldiers. Once a week or once every two weeks they would be in the PTT building, but they would simply drive up. It wasn't really a headquarters that was equipped with soldiers and maps, no. That was somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: In relation to your meetings with the civil authorities, can you recall the names of the individuals that you specifically dealt with?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mayor, when we arrived, if I remember correctly, that was Osman. He was about 50. There was also a Hamdija, who was the deputy mayor. And I forget the name, but we could trace that in my previous statement. There was also a former veterinarian or physician who was involved. Those were the three main people.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And it would be fair to say, would it not, that in your role as liaison officer, you would primarily deal with leaders in the community on the civilian side? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning that's true for the first two months, because I had a colleague there who focused primarily on contact with the military, but because of various circumstances, this colleague was transferred back to the Netherlands, and I -- maintaining contact with the military was added to my responsibilities, or rather, I assumed that responsibility as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, you've given some evidence in relation to the difficulties that were observed by the DutchBat in relation to food supply into the enclave. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you state your question a bit more clearly, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll be a bit more specific. The fact is while you were there will in the Srebrenica enclave there were difficulties in terms of humanitarian aid and food coming into the enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And what your evidence was on, I believe, Monday or Tuesday, the BSA was certainly responsible in some respects in creating that difficulty. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I said that. I remember saying that the convoy system depended on permits issued from Pale and that I didn't know how that worked in Pale. From below, we would report to Major Nikolic that we were requesting a convoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Condon. I take it that when you are referring -- when you're using the acronym BSA, you're referring to Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The VRS or the BSA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, because VRS is VRS, and BSA is more taken to be -- to mean Bosnian Serb authorities. So -- yes, Mr. Nicholls. So we need to be clear. If you're referring to the armed forces or the army itself, you refer to as VRS, as we have been referring it -- to it throughout. Otherwise, BSA would be Bosnian Serb authorities to me. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd request transcript references. I think Your Honours has made an oral order about this earlier that parties are supposed to say which date and page to say they're referring. I don't think there's a reason to say you said it Monday or Tuesday because we all have transcripts immediately and there's plenty of time to prepare for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the second point I was getting to. You need to refer the witness to the specific part of the transcript where he's supposed to have stated what you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Perhaps, I'll take him specifically to the particular issue that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mind you, he doesn't remember because he went exactly to mentioning again Pale which he had mentioned before in that context, but let's be a little bit more precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I have at page 41, line 8 to lines 22 on the 19th of September that there was reference to obstruction of aid convoys, but I'll put the question again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, in particular you gave evidence about the fact that a black market had emerged as a result of that. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that -- or did you have any suspicions as to the role of any of the military leaders in the 28th Division being involved in that, in the black market?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any proof. I think it's clear that there were earnings through the black market, and whether that's associated with the military leaders of the 28th Division, I suspect that there was, but actual proof, especially because soldiers sometimes exited the enclave, and if there was smuggling, it happened from Tuzla toward the enclave or from Zepa toward the enclave. On occasion that -- might not be present in the enclave and he might say he'd been to Zepa briefly. So that people would stay elsewhere and possibly smuggle. And about the leaders, well, I have suspicions but I can't prove it. Once I attended a banquet at the mayor's place that was like a four or five-star banquet while the rest of the population was really suffering.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown 1D0019. I'm not sure if it's 000 or 00, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, at page 3 of this document in English and also page 3 in the B/C/S version, but obviously for you, Colonel Boering, I'll direct your attention to page 3 in the English version, the third paragraph --

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see a document in English. I see a document in a different language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You should be able to -- no. It's in B/C/S as well the one we got now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I see the English one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need one in English and one in B/C/S so that the accused can follow, please. At least on one screen. On a screen that is more accessible to the accused it should be in B/C/S. If you need time to organise this, we can have the break and we do it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: If that's easier, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. It's past our time anyway. So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now, and thank you for understanding, Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were very anxious to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: One minor issue. Is the Prosecution going to give us copies of this witness's notes he's been referring to since he started testifying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it's the Prosecution that will give you those. You need to ask the witness to make them -- or put a question. I thought this had been referred to the witness. He had agreed. So maybe you can thrash it out now --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Obviously, I don't have the notes but I don't have any objection to anything being provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you start again, Ms. Condon -- or you can remain seated. Just one question to Mr. Meek. Have you been provided with the -- okay. So you don't have any further problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, for your cooperation. Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, do you have that document in front of you in English?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see English text in front of me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And I want to draw your attention to the third paragraph on the English document beginning with "The increasing mistrust ..." Do you see that there? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'll read it out to you: "The increasing mistrust felt by the citizens of Srebrenica for the civilian and military leadership was encouraged by the unequal allocation and manipulation of goods provided by humanitarian aid. Naser Oric and municipal officials Osman Suljic, Adem Salihovic, and Hamdija Fejzic were linked to this. There is information indicating that these men smuggled humanitarian aid, weapons, oil, et cetera, and that they collaborated with members of UNPROFOR and even with the aggressor in their smuggling activities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we -- can you tell us, please, what document we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: The actual document -- forgive me, Your Honour. I should have indicated that from the outset. This is a document that is addressed to General Delic. It's dated on the original the 23rd of February, 1995, and it is from Brigadier General Jasarevic. It's a summary on the fall of Srebrenica and Zepa, which raises obvious questions in terms of the accuracy of it being the 23rd of February, 1995. It simply cannot be because it refers to events that occur in April, May, June, July of 1995. So I wouldn't imagine there would be much dispute that that must be an error on the original document, and of course the original document's in evidence as well, Your Honour, in the sense that it's part of the Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Am I right that we have seen this document before already? Have we?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Not as far as I'm aware, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Boering, I don't want you to make any comment on what is alleged there in relation to collaboration with members of UNPROFOR. I don't expect you to agree with that. I want your comment on what it says there about the involvement of Mr. Oric and the civilian authorities. You would not dispute that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that there was mistrust towards the authorities, towards the leadership, was a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. I'm sorry to stop you so abruptly, Colonel, but I hear that Mr. Borovcanin has got a problem. Speak up, Mr. Borovcanin, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think these documents are not synchronised, the one in English and the translation. They're not on the same page, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for pointing that out. I had the suspicion of that, actually, because one is page 2 and the other is page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: The B/C/S document is page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know the language. If you -- yes. Stop. Stop there. So we're looking at the first full paragraph on that page after the first three lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay? All right. Thank you. Thank you for pointing that out. Whenever that happens, please draw our attention straight away. I thank you. Yes. Sorry. Colonel, do you wish us to repeat the question that was put to you, or do you still remember it and would like to proceed with your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to proceed with my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question whether the mistrust was increasing was unclear in the enclave. I was aware of a very strong, firm leadership about -- and contacts with the opposition was not appreciated. Within the enclave I also experienced this. Whether people gathered wealth and goods, there was a suspicion towards that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask the question again simply because in my view it hasn't been answered sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, what I asked you was in light of what I read to you in that document, you would not dispute the allegation that the military leadership and the civilian leadership were themselves linked to the black market?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect that they were linked, but it's not more than a suspicion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, you gave some evidence in relation to helicopter flights that were coming into the enclave. You recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Just so there's no dispute about this, the concern in relation to the helicopter flights was because they were a source of bringing -- the ABiH bringing in military hardware, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a suspicion towards that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And while you yourself didn't see it, that was the source of the concern, wasn't it, that they were bringing in arms? You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's answered the question already.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you would agree, Colonel Boering, by the end of DutchBat III's time in the enclave, there was more helicopter activity, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the middle of April, May, June, those activities increased.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And you would also agree, wouldn't you, that from May, June, July, 1995, the enclave was becoming increasingly militarised, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only change I saw in the demeanour -- the military demeanour of ABiH was that I noticed newer uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So your evidence is that during that period your only observations were new uniforms, but new weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you to your evidence in relation to the first meeting at the Hotel Fontana on the 11th of July, 1995. Do you recall the evidence you've given in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Specifically, your evidence was that as to who initiated the meeting, you cannot recall whether or not the initiative had come from the VRS or the DutchBat side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I said that this was discussed in the previous trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. You -- what you say in this trial, however, is, "I cannot precisely --" this is at page 9, lines 18 to 22, Your Honour. "I cannot precisely indicate whether the initiative had come from the VRS or the DutchBat side. In any case, it was a meeting where we arrived, we were welcomed, and where we were expected. People were expecting us in order to hold the meeting." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I said, and the word "expect" was related to the --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'll just interrupt you, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VRS --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm explaining what I mean by "expected."

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But I'm not asking you for an explanation. Please simply listen to the question. The question was: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were told by Ms. Condon what you testified here on page -- line -- page 9, lines 18 to 22. Basically, the question is the following: Having heard this read out to you, do you stand by it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And in your first statement that you made -- this is at page 6, Your Honour, of the witness's first statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: ERN number -- this is 28th of September, 1995. The exhibit number is ID00017.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So could we see it? Therefore, could we have it on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: This is at page 6, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Oh, 1D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a hard copy available anyone?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I think it's just coming up now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So let's start from here. Colonel, do you remember giving a statement to -- can we go back one page, please? Go back one page. First page. Yes. Can you see the first page, the front cover page of this statement or this document, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can see it, and that was 11 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I vaguely remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that was going to be my next question. So he vaguely remembers it. So please go ahead with your questions, Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: On page 6 of that statement, in the second paragraph, you said this: "At one point we received a request from Bratunac, from the DutchBat hostages to have a meeting with Mladic in Bratunac." Now, is that correct? Do you agree that's what you said in your first statement?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it written there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And you agree that that's what -- that's correct? That's what you said in your first statement.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You then went on to say: "He himself had requested a meeting ..." That being -- "he" being General Mladic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, because I can't see it in the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. The line that begins "He himself had requested a meeting." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If it assists counsel, I have all of his statements in hard copy. If it assists, I have a binder that has all of the statements in it. I don't think it has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much for that, but we could zoom in the second paragraph on page 6, and actually, we're just referring to one sentence. "He himself had requested a meeting," and it's being suggested this referred to General Mladic, and you're being asked to confirm that this is what you stated in your statement of 1995, whenever it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's my statement from 1995, and as far as I can remember, that's how I said it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And what you say now is that that specific memory you had that it was General Mladic that requested the meeting you are not so sure you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Memories fade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Because in effect, Colonel Boering, the fact was that when you arrived at the Hotel Fontana, there was no expectation that it was General Mladic that you were to be meeting, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a meeting, but whether General Mladic would be there, that was something we couldn't expect.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, because your lieutenant commander Karremans didn't in fact know that he was speaking to General Mladic, did he? Originally. You're nodding? You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He didn't know that he would be speaking to General Mladic, not that he -- because the way it's in the transcript and the way I heard you state it, it's as if General -- Commander Karremans. He didn't know he was speaking to General Mladic so he didn't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: It's both, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what you meant is that he didn't know beforehand who he would be speaking to.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'll break it down.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You agree, Colonel Boering, that on your way to Bratunac you had the three of you, yourself, Lieutenant Colonel Karremans, Major Rave, no expectation that you would be meeting with General Mladic. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And secondly, that you in fact were the only one of the three of you who knew that it was in fact general Mladic who you were speaking to in that meeting originally. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment the meeting had already started and I entered later, I saw Lieutenant Colonel Karremans speaking with General Mladic, and at that moment Lieutenant Colonel Karremans had not yet figured out that was General Mladic. I thought it was General Zivanovic for a moment. I knew the latter vaguely, so I checked briefly with my interpreter, Petar, and he said, yes, of course, that's Mladic. And then I communicated to -- I communicated to Lieutenant Colonel Karremans whom he was speaking with. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. So it follows from that -- you agree, then, that when you made that statement that it was General Mladic that requested the meeting, that simply cannot be right? Your Honour, I'm not sure if the interpretation is particularly slow, but I have some concerns about the -- perhaps the amount of time that the witness is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what you're saying in English is being translated into Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the witness is waiting until it is over before he starts answering. And that's how it has been going since he started giving evidence. So we have to be patient. It takes time, I know, but patience is a --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Virtue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And he's trying to recall questions to specific events from a very long time ago, so I think counsel should be patient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the other thing you mentioned, I was allowing -- giving the witness the opportunity to try and answer your question, I still can't understand how the conclusion that you put to him follows from what we have been hearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I'll break it down, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, because it says so, it follows from that you agree that when you made that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That it was General Mladic that requested the meeting, that simply cannot be right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No, I appreciate what Your Honour is saying. I'll break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- or a radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- conclusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Mladic would like to see General Karremans. Anyway, rephrase the question --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- in whatever way you like, and with the witness I'll not ask him to speed up his answers because I don't know what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, when you made that statement in September, 1995, that it was General Mladic requesting the meeting, it follows from that, does it not, that you knew that General Mladic wanted to see DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on that question that is rather complex to me, the way I see it now, the invitation was not directed personally by General Mladic that we should stop over, and how that relates this testimony to my testimony in 1995, my memory doesn't go back that far in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make it clear and stop this here. So let's divide it into two parts. Part one of your statement way back in 1995 is that the request for a meeting did not originate from DutchBat but originated from the Serbian side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And would it be a fair statement to say that your conclusion that it was General Mladic who had summoned that meeting and no one else was because when you ultimately ended up in the Fontana Hotel it was General Mladic that you met and spoke with? Would that be a fair statement? In other words, your conclusion that it was General Mladic did not originate from any hard fact, any telex or radio communication from General Mladic or from someone mentioning General Mladic's name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I agree were that. I confirm it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Tell me this, Colonel Boering: You were in what was known as Section 5; is that right? That was your division in DutchBat? Yes, that's right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And tell me if I've got this wrong, but the procedure when DutchBat wanted to initiate a meeting with the VRS was that you would use Petar, the interpreter. Is that correct? To arrange the meeting.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were various options. Either through Petar or through Yellow Bridge that one of the Serbs would contact one of our posts, or in this case of our soldiers that had been taken prisoner, via radio messages. There were various options.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And one of them was to use Petar, is that correct, the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that on the afternoon of the 11th of July, 1995, you were in fact asked by Lieutenant Colonel Karremans to contact Petar and arrange a meeting with the VRS at the Hotel Fontana? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Because Lieutenant Colonel Karremans has been asked about this. This is at page 11256 to 11257 in the trial of Jokic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Makes me remember Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The rule on that case and in other cases here is that a fact is put to the witness and the witness answers based on that fact but that witnesses are not pitted against each other. There's no need to say where -- that you're contradicting another witness, and my motion would be just that the statement is put to the witness and then asked if it's correct or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the procedure here, Ms. Condon, so it's easy. You just rephrase your question without referring to any particular witness, especially in this case, who happens to be his superior at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, if there were evidence to the effect that you were asked to organise that meeting through Petar the interpreter on this afternoon, would you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, again, "if there were evidence." I think just the proposition should be put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't find -- I don't -- I don't think the question as such is objectionable. We can proceed. Please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Shall I perhaps repeat the question, Colonel Boering?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: If there were evidence to the effect that you were asked to organise the meeting on the 11th of July, 1995, at Bratunac through Petar the interpreter, would you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there's evidence, then that's evidence. We were in touch with Petar repeatedly during that period about various meetings, but regarding this specific case, no, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps we should just establish from the outset, Colonel Boering. Your evidence has been that you missed perhaps the initial part of the first meeting at the Hotel Fontana; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I missed the first little part of the meeting at Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. Now -- however, insofar as what we watched on the video in this court, you were present for the entire part of what we saw on the video; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do remember that I wasn't present at the first part, so relating that to the video, then it's not a complete recording.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No, no, no. That wasn't my question.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No, no. My question was quite simple. In terms of what we saw on the video in this court, were you present for what we saw on the video; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me. It's being put to you that when we saw the video relating to the first Bratunac Hotel Fontana meeting, it seems that from beginning to the end of what we saw in that video you were present. So you are asked to either confirm -- you're asked to explain why this is so if you, according to yourself, were not present for the initial part of the meeting? Do you have an explanation why the video shows you present throughout? There's a very simple answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the video recording starts at a certain point, yes, I'm there at that point. And if the meeting started before that, then that's not on the video. I'm firmly convinced of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. And I appreciate that you've chosen to have an interpreter in Dutch today, but you wouldn't dispute the fact that you're fluent in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He's answered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He answered that yesterday or the day before.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'll be more specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Although he didn't acknowledge he's fluent. He has -- he's got sufficient knowledge of English to make him understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. Insofar as the communications between the interpreter and -- I should say between General Mladic to the interpreter were concerned in English, you understood the communications between those two insofar as the interpreter was speaking in English?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent that I could hear what the interpreter was telling Lieutenant Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you say that that was largely because of where you were positioned during the meeting at the Hotel Fontana; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Insofar as your memory as to what was said, do you recall General Mladic saying to Lieutenant Colonel Karremans, "What do you want? You asked for a meeting. Speak up."

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He could have said something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic was rather annoyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, if the witness could be shown P02048, at page 19 of that document. This is the transcript of the video that we've seen at the Hotel Fontana. And unfortunately I don't have a line reference, Your Honour, as to where the conversation begins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- we could actually refer to the video itself if the segment could be identified.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd prefer to actually take the witness to the transcript rather than show the video again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: At the middle of -- at the middle of page 19 there is a -- where it begins with General Mladic speaking. Yes? Now, you have it in B/C/S on your left. You should it in English on your right.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see any English yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No, it's all right, Colonel Boering. Neither do I. Right. You see that now in English --

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.
