utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- Colonel Boering? Once again you see that in fact it's in bold. "What do you want? You asked for a meeting. Speak up." I'll ask you again because your answer was he could have said that, but you see there that according to the transcript he did say that. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Does that assist your memory at all in terms of the question of DutchBat initiating this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That doesn't -- isn't something that perhaps jogs your memory in any way that you might accept that it in fact was DutchBat that initiated the first meeting at Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Despite what it says there in the transcript? I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Further down Lieutenant Colonel Karremans then goes on to convey this: Firstly, that he'd spoken to -- he had a talk to General Nikolai two hours ago. Now, I think you were asked about this in your evidence in-chief. General Nikolai was the Chief of Staff at the Sarajevo headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Nikolai's specific role is not rock solid in my memory at this time, but he was in Sarajevo and he was our liaison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One second. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the page in B/C/S does not tally with the English page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I can't help you much. Yeah, yeah. Okay. Tell us now. Yes, of course. I fully understand. I wouldn't be able to notice that. That's why I told the accused earlier on if it doesn't tally, let us know. It still doesn't tally according to you, Mr. Borovcanin? Yes. Can we go back to the previous page in B/C/S, towards the bottom of it, please? Yes. At the end. No. No. No, it's not. I can't -- I can't help you because I don't understand the language. So someone needs to help us there if you insist on seeing the -- because I thought that basically you had finished your series of questions on this. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I suggest to proceed because the accused can follow through the interpretation, because you read out the passage and it will be interpreted for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I still do have some more questions in relation to this page that we are referring to. I just point out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If somebody gives me a hard copy I'll give you the correct page. I mean, if somebody has a hard copy of this statement in B/C/S I will tell you exactly where it is, but in the meantime, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: The third aspect of what Lieutenant Colonel Karremans specifically says to General Mladic is that he'd been ordered by BH command to take care of the refugees. You recall him conveying that to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time upon reading it I can imagine that he said it, but it's not -- it's not etched in my memory that he did indeed say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But you accept that it's on the transcript and that was said?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you also accept, then, that it was also said that he was there at the request of the BH command to negotiate or ask for the withdrawal of the battalion. That's obviously DutchBat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the words of Lieutenant Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But he was also there to negotiate or ask for the withdrawal of the refugees. You agree with that, that that's what it says there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you also may recall that there was a reference to General Janvier. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read it, but a true memory, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. But you accept that -- it appears at page 26, Your Honour. You accept that when the transcript says, "That's why General Nikolai asked me or more by General Janvier and he received orders from General Janvier," you accept that's what on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we need a witness to confirm to us what's in a transcript? The transcript is the transcript. It speaks for itself. So if you want to ask him about the contents, you can ask him about the contents, but still don't stay repeating the same question all the time, do you accept this is what the transcript says? Do you accept that this is in the transcript? It's there. We can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour, but the witness did initially -- didn't give that concession. He said it could have been said without me showing him the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the question was: Is it in the transcript? And the answer, I don't think I need Colonel Boering to deal me whether it's in the transcript or not. I can look at the transcript and I can see it for myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, who to your knowledge, Colonel Boering, who was General Janvier?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zagreb. A commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Were you, prior to attending at the Hotel Fontana, were you in fact aware that there had been any communication between Lieutenant Colonel Karremans and General Nikolai?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that Lieutenant Colonel Karremans was in touch with several of the powers that were, but with who and the substance of those communications, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate you wouldn't know what the substance of those communications were. Were you aware that a fax had been received on -- at 6.00 -- 1842, so about a quarter to 7.00 at DutchBat from the headquarters at Sarajevo? Perhaps without -- without answering that, perhaps, if the witness could be shown, Your Honour, 1D00026. Now, you'll see that the first page of this was a Rule 70 document originally, Your Honour, but it's been -- was on the EDS, so it's a document that's been disclosed by the Prosecution. The first page I don't need you to look at. The second page is what I want you to look at. All right. Can you see that there, Colonel Boering, in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: One moment, please. It's possible, but I don't remember this.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. But you can see that if we go through it it is dated the 11th of July, 1995, and it appears to have the time 18.27 around -- do you see that at the top corner? The top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand corner I see the moment it arrived which was at 0340 in the morning, so it took longer for a fax to reach DutchBat. The moment something is signed isn't necessarily the moment it arrives.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt -- Colonel Boering --

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm explaining when the fax arrived at DutchBat and if you look at the very top you see a date July 1995 followed by a time of the arrival at DutchBat. That means that was when the fax arrived and was printed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- there will be a lot of confusion. It is activated. My microphone is switched on, but maybe I was keeping away from it. All right. Let's proceed. Your next question, Ms. Condon, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, I wasn't asking you for your opinion as to when this fax arrived at DutchBat, simply that it has a date on it, the 11th of July, 1995. There is a time in the right corner, 18.27B. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That it is from acting commander Gobillard. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And the subject matter is orders for defence of DutchBat and protection of refugees in Srebrenica. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Then there are a number points that are described in the document, and at the very bottom of the document you'll see, and it is upside down, but there is a line, and at the very bottom left-hand corner - thank you - the 11th of July, 1995, 18.42. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And then at the top, as you say, it is -- the date is -- this is again at the top of the document, normally the date is obscured, but it has July, 1995, 03.40, comcen DutchBat. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And as you read that, your understanding is that indicates the time at which this document was received at DutchBat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I assume. And the bottom side has another time, but here you see comcen DutchBat, which indicates the time the document arrived. Where at the lower side of the page I do not see this added. But I'm not 100 per cent sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So it is in fact possible from reading the document, is it not, that the bottom inscription of the 11th of July, 1995, 18.42, could indicate the time at which the fax came in to DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can recall is that contacts with faxes was very difficult. Printing faxes was difficult, and that it used to take a very long time before faxes would come in and be printed out. That's the only thing I can recall. So there may have been a delay somewhere in the chain.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a moment. This seems to be page 4, according to the communication record, the very first top line -- the first line on the top. Can I see again the one on the bottom, please. All right. Now, this is part of a larger document. Could we see the previous page of this document if it is part of this document. So this is where this document starts, and the next page is the fax -- or the fax that we've seen. And is there another page --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour, but, Your Honour, there are two pages that are attached to the first page that we are looking at, and I was obviously going to take the witness to those pages because that's the significance of what I say about when the fax arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I was trying to see clearer in this, but I don't know what to make out of it. Yes, Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Would you accept, Colonel Boering, that the way in which this message reads is akin to an order to the recipient, being the commander of DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is an order, an instruction.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, you -- I mean, you have been cross-examined about this document before. You can recall that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'm not sure how Mr. Karnavas would feel about that, but when you were asked those questions, you were asked -- this is at page 984, Your Honour, of Jokic, that you described them as instructions which we received for our information. This is at lines 22 to 25. But you had a specific recollection that Lieutenant Colonel Karremans telephoned Tuzla about this document.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those proceedings this has been discussed, but I do not have it that precisely or clearly in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But I can put the specific question and answer to you if you want me to, Colonel Boering, but do you accept that in the past you have said that you recall Lieutenant Colonel Karremans telephoning Tuzla about this document that we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I made that statement in the past, then obviously this is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So if you go, then, to page -- the next page of the document, which will be page 2. Now, if you blow this up. This is in fact the document that we saw yesterday. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's the letter from Lieutenant Colonel Karremans to the various authorities. Now, at the top of this document you'll see that again the date is obscured, and it has the time 03.35, comcen DutchBat. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And then this document is identified with a number at the top, 1561750. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see a document number.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: It's all right. Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The very first line which is the communication data.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt. If it helps my friend we have another copy of the same document which was disclosed. It does have an ERN and it does shows the date in the top left-hand corner if my friend would like to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it also have the handwriting and the markings?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, it appears to. But I'm afraid the copy I have has a lot of my notes on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What date does it show, the top left?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It says 12 July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And then you'll see the final page, the next page, again same thing. It's the second page of Colonel Karremans' letter. It has 3.38, comcen DutchBat, page 3.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, these three pages all have, as you can see, Colonel Boering, that same heading at the top with the date obscured but beginning with 3.40. You say we know 12th of July, 1995, 03.40. Does that suggest to you that that was a faxed -- that was a document that was faxed in the early hours of the morning? An outgoing fax, not an incoming fax?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect looking at the document that it concerns an outgoing fax.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Right. So in fact, when we go back to the first document, the HQ UNPROFOR Sarajevo document, that when you're reading from the top line of that, the information data on there is reflecting not an incoming fax but an outgoing fax. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it would seem like, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. So -- so that we have this clear, it is not the case that the order from acting commander Gobillard was received on the 12th of July, 1995, at 03.40.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this certainly would not lead to me concluding as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But as you've said, you yourself weren't aware from Lieutenant Colonel Karremans of any specific order that he received prior to the meeting at Hotel Fontana? You agree with that? You yourself didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But if you accept from this document if it was in fact received on the 11th of July, 1995, at 18.42 into the DutchBat headquarters, that from this document Lieutenant Colonel Karremans did in fact have orders prior to the first meeting at Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this fax arrived to DutchBat and was read by commander Karremans before the meeting, then this would be the case, but I had no confirmation whether the fax had come in and whether he had read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about your role in choosing the civil representative. Now, what you say is that you knew Nesib Mandic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You described him as somebody that you were relatively often in touch with; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But you also have made it clear that he wasn't somebody you considered to be a community leader; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But you've also agreed that in your role as a liaison officer it was primarily civil and community leaders that you did in fact have contact with; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. However, besides my work, I also had to coordinate civilian projects, and it was part of my job to have contacts with people of the civil community. I was, for instance, in contact with the heads of several schools, and I would visit these schools personally. He was the director of one of the schools. And in my capacity, I was in regular contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, what happened was that in between the second and the third meeting you sought to find further representatives; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The desire of General Mladic is to have more representatives. That is correct. And DutchBat worked on this. That is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to my personally -- as to me personally, I didn't walk or drive around trying to find additional people.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, there was also an attempt by some of the civil representatives back at DutchBat headquarters to make contact with the Bosnian government authorities, wasn't there, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, you had a specific recollection in your first statement -- Your Honour, the first statement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: This is the first statement of the 28th of September, 1995. 1D00017, at page 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: The fifth paragraph where it reads: "We left again about half an hour later. At the compound our spokesman found two other people to act as spokespersons, a man and a woman. Next morning these spokespersons attempted to contact the government in Sarajevo, but without success." That's what you said in your first statement, Colonel Boering; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have been working on establishing contacts. I myself also tried to establish contacts with Tuzla. So there have been attempts to make telephone communications both in the night and in the following morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But what your evidence is is that -- you say that those attempts were unsuccessful; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At least for as much as I am concerned personally. And I cannot say whether those two individuals have been successful in establishing contacts. I don't know how it is exactly worded in the statement, but I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You can't remember them being successful in terms of making contact. That's what you're saying; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can not remember the outcome, the result of that telephone communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the witness be shown 1D00024, at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, in that second paragraph -- I'll read it to you. And Your Honour can see that I'm reading from the national institute Dutch -- the Dutch government report on Srebrenica. That's identifying the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree with that description of the document, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I take counsel's word for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Where it reads: "Although an accurate reconstruction is made difficult because of the usual problems of conflicting memories, the possibility emerges that one or more committee members also tried to get instructions from either Sarajevo or Tuzla. Both Omanovic and Mandzic later referred to such attempts. The notes in Rave's notebook of those days refer to a telephone conversation with Muratovic, the minister who was responsible for the relations with the United Nations, and the request for instructions from him, President Izetbegovic and Prime Minister Silajdzic. Mandzic later told intelligence officers of the 2nd Corps of the ABiH that he had had contact with Silajdzic at about 10.00 hours on July 12."

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: What time was the final meeting on the 12th of July at the Hotel Fontana, Colonel Boering?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was around 10.00. In the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So that in fact would seem to suggest that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- that there had at least been some conversation between Nesib Mandzic and a member of the BiH government -- oh, sorry, I'll withdraw that. Intelligence officers of the 2nd Corps of the ABiH prior to the final meeting. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it's described here, I don't have any perception of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you to your evidence in relation to the military strength of the 28th Division of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And if the witness could be shown, Your Honour, ID 00020. This is at page 2 of that document. And I should just indicate, Your Honour, this is a document, a UNMO document. The author of it is an UNMO, right? And it is a postscript to the -- it's entitled "Postscript to events of Srebrenica." Just further down that document. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Just so your evidence is clear, what you say is that the 28th Division of the ABiH had no more than a thousand members; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to a nucleus of well-trained soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. But you've based that estimate before, haven't you, on whether or not the member concerned had a new weapon or a new uniform? You agree with that? That's the criteria you've used in the past?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not alone in a battalion. There's also somebody from intelligence, and that person provides the information and analyses it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Colonel Boering. I'm not sure how that's a response to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I might have missed it, but was there a -- is there a reference to his testimony that he's given in this trial about the military strength that --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'll give it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know what this is relating to that he said here. That's a little unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it he's simply being asked questions about the military strength of ABiH. I haven't heard so far any cross-reference to anything else except what is -- appears on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's just that she said, "I'll take you to your evidence in relation to the military strength," and I wasn't sure where that -- where that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There you have a right to ask for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: What you said in this trial on page 57, lines 3 to 4, was that the weaponry that the ABiH had had were outdated. The 19th of September.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm reminding you of your previous evidence, Colonel Boering, that in this court, what you've said is that the weaponry that the ABiH had was outdated. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you. And that they did not have state-of-the-art military equipment. These are your words.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, I'm repeating your evidence back to you, Colonel Boering. It's not a question of whether or not it's possible. What you said on the 19th of September, 2006, at lines 1 to 4, 57 -- page 57, you were asked: "If you can be a little more specific what types of weapons you're referring to if you can be." Answer: "Machine-guns, rifles, handguns, they were often relatively outdated, not ordinarily state-of-the-art military equipment." Now, is that true? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And as far as you're aware, that's a correct assessment of the state of the 28th Division's military strength?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So, if there were evidence to the effect that in April or May the 28th Division had new uniforms and Kalashnikovs that looked brand new, you would not agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those are firearms and uniforms. I mentioned the uniforms and some small arms, but that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, but my specific question to you is that if there were evidence that in April and May the 28th Division had new, brand new Kalashnikov rifles, you would disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You certainly would. All right. Now, just having a look at the document that's in front of you where it says under the heading "ABiH," and you can see there that it is written: "Not known, however the usual estimate of 10 per cent of population would give a force of approximately 4.000." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You would, I suspect, too, disagree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just ask him whether he agrees or he doesn't, because the way you phrased it is --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, my pleasure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Shall I ask it again, Colonel Boering?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, you would like me to ask the question again, or -- yes?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Where it says: "ABiH. Not known, however the usual estimate of 10 per cent of the population would give a force of approximately 4.000," do you agree or disagree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in which context this should be placed. The estimate, I mean. I would assume a good thousand troops that are the nucleus. And where you get that 10 per cent as the usual estimate, I don't know. You'd have to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, but this is document that's been -- Your Honour, I see the time, and I can indicate that I will certainly have no more than 15 minutes after the break. Once I've concluded with this topic I have one other and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a break now, 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I recognise Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just wanted to put on the record the document where I read the date 12 July from is number 531 is exactly the same document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. The document I read the date 12 July from is 65 ter number 531 is actually the same document that I used in my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Nicholls, for that information. Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, I was asking you about that document that you have there in front of you. I want to -- you to have a look at page A-2 of that document. That's how it reads on the original document. I hope that assists the court ushers.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's there. I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Just at the bottom. You'll see there's a reference to 9 July 1995. And just before I take you to the content of that paragraph, you recall that on the 9th of July, 1995, you had two meetings that day.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meetings with the ABiH, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. You had a meeting in the morning with Ramiz Becirevic, the leader of the 28th Division, and then a further meeting with Osman Suljic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that he personally met with these two persons?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to that first meeting with the military, there was a fairly tense situation, wasn't there, for DutchBat in withdrawing, because you were being fired on by the ABiH in the withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether we were being fired at I don't know, but there were tensions between the ABiH and DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, you already gave evidence about the fact that Private Rensen died. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And wasn't it the case that OP H, that's the one -- the observation post closest -- closest to the town of Srebrenica was actually attacked at one point by the BiH?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that last bit. I do remember that there was a post where one of our vehicles was prevented from moving any more under -- under threat by the RPG, and I spoke to the mayor, and after that the vehicle was able to move on. So there was tension and there were threats, but I did not personally see an exchange of fire or anything similar to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, you're familiar with the UNMO situation reports that would be sent out from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I was. Sometimes I was not. They have their own reporting lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be fair to say, would it not, that much of the information or some, at least, of the information from these reports would come from DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: A combination of data from themselves and from us. Generally they reported -- they submitted their own reports and DutchBat submitted its own reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Just going back to the meeting of the 9th of July. Would you accept that in the course of that meeting that you had -- DutchBat had made a request that the BiH would not hinder any of their withdrawal movements? This is DutchBat's withdrawal movements.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: DutchBat did indeed request freedom of movement to operate, not only to withdraw but also to advance freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But you'll see there in that document you have in front of you the meeting is described like this: "In a meeting between DutchBat, Ramiz --" sorry. "In a meeting between DutchBat, Ramiz and Osman involve mutual recriminations ..." Do you accept that's what happened in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was suspicion and mistrust.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: DutchBat LO, is that you, liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I was alone at the DutchBat meeting, I don't know. But it could indeed be a reference to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But we've established it's you. You accept that you were present at this meeting on the 9th of July?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So: "DutchBat LO accused Ramiz of ordering his troops to remove the weapons in the custody of B Coy." B Company. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But you accept that that's how the meeting is represented there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this coming up with Ramiz. I suspect that we addressed a weapon collection point and that the Bravo Company wanted those weapons. I believe that that is an inaccurate reflection of the meeting. Ramiz repeatedly asked for the arms from the weapons collection point. I don't believe he ever wanted or demanded our arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. So when -- what about where it says there: "Ramiz, however, stated that he'd been ordered to demand the return of these weapons and those of the Dutch but had not bothered as he anticipated the Dutch response." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Question?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I just put the question. Where it says Ramiz stated that he had been ordered to demand the return of these weapons and those of the Dutch but had not bothered as he had anticipated the Dutch response, is that true? Is that what happened in the meeting? Did Ramiz make that statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's answered the question in as far as it's related to Bosnian Muslim weapons proper, yes. As regards DutchBat weapons, never. This is his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, and just the question I don't think is completely fair as to whether he made what statement because as I read it, Ramiz, he didn't bother to make the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But from the document you can also read it that he never bothered to ask for the return of their own weapons, of the Bosnian Muslim weapons, and that's not what the witness stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Could the witness be shown P00500, Your Honour. This is a situation report dated the 9th of July. Or the heading is the 9th of July, 1995. Yes. And the second page. That's the page. Yes, sorry. The next page after that. And just further down. That's it. Now, what you say is that you had no awareness of the ABiH firing upon any of the observation posts of DutchBat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Have a read, please, of the paragraph that begins: "Update 082059B July '95. Report from DutchBat indicates that their OPs U and S are under attack by the BSA. And to make matters worse, they are also being prevented by the BiH from leaving these areas." Does this accord with what you understood the situation to be at the time, Colonel Boering?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to reflect on this in its proper context. You asked me -- in the English text I read "BSA attack on DutchBat."

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: If you're reading that, that's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based -- based on your question, I'm inferring OP -- "and to make matters worse, they are also being prevented by the BiH situation at this time." Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, "while OPs U and S were being attacked bit BSA, and to make matters worse, they are also being prevented by the BiH from leaving these areas." "They" being DutchBat. Now, does that accord with the situation as you understood it at the time?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier here this morning, tensions existed regarding the freedom of movement, and in one case I went there myself to try to arrange such freedom of movement. So, yes, there was an unwillingness on the part of the BiH to allow us freedom of movement, and that made it difficult for us to operate.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But you will agree there is a clear difference, is there not, between restrictions on freedom of movement and being fired upon. That's obvious.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I mentioned earlier that I don't remember the BiH firing at us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps if you can have a look at ii of that document where it says: "DutchBat OP H is being fired upon by the BiH." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But you would say that doesn't accord with your recollection of the events at that time?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as you can see in the text, Ramiz mentions that this did not happen at his orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Were you at B Company on the 8th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Around the 8th or the 9th I was with the Bravo Company.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But do you have any recollection of the BiH blocking the compound of B Company at this time?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I walked out of the gate several times towards the PTT building, so I did not see a blockade there. I did see a huge number of refugees in front of the gate.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But you see there it says on that document at i that "they were out just blocking the compound of B Company". Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see where it says that, but I did not witness that with my own eyes, and I don't remember a lot of UN observers walking around the city at that time. So I don't know what they base this statement on. You'd need to ask them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You're not suggesting, are you, that the information that's contained in the UNMO situation reports is unreliable? You're not suggesting that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You would just say that the information that is contained here doesn't reflect your observations on the 8th of July, 1995, at B Company.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I walked around there myself several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: And when I walked around there, I did not see any UN observers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: What about BiH armed soldiers on the 8th of July? Did you see any of them walking around B Company? You would have noticed them, I presume.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question is what a BiH armed soldier is. To give you an example, the mayor up to that point had no involvement with the army at all to his own indication. I saw him at a certain point, and he was wearing a uniform and he was armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Well, perhaps if we go to the next page of this document and we can ascertain what a -- the description "armed soldier" means, because you'll see there at the top of the page it says: "Update 0821408B July 95. Below is information received from DutchBat concerning our last update ..." So you would agree that this makes it fairly clear that this is information coming from DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't mean to say, Ms. Condon, that every information coming from DutchBat necessarily was something that he personally was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Personally was aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- was personally aware of. So perhaps you could address any questions as to his personal knowledge, please, feel free to do so, but don't attribute to him a universal knowledge of DutchBat acquired information.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You see the second Roman numeral: "The situation at B Company is also stable but a little tense. There are about 30 BiH armed soldiers and a lot of civilians walking around the compound." Now, did you see that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember those figures, but there were armed soldiers walking around the compound, but I walked around there freely and did not feel threatened.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, I didn't ask you if you felt threatened. We'll move on to a meeting that you attended on the 10th of July, 1995, with Lieutenant Colonel Karremans. That was a meeting that was held in the evening; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the meeting with the BiH in the PTT building at which the mayor was also present.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that meeting took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of at the time of that meeting seeing about 1.000 to 1.500 combatants in town at the time?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to take you back to your movements after the final meeting at the Hotel Fontana on the 12th of July, 1995. Your evidence is that after that final meeting you returned to Bratunac to get a clearer picture of what had been agreed upon. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And in particular, you wanted to -- you and Major Rave went back to knock out some details in particular in relation to the question of fuel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe Major Rave came along. It was primarily about fuel and the general transport plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. If at -- again, in your second statement -- Your Honour, this is the statement dated the -- it's sworn on the 10th of February, 1998, number 1D00018.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it a sworn statement, this one?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Or perhaps I shouldn't use the word "sworn." It's what I'm used to. Perhaps "affirmed" is a better expression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's just that it would be the first sworn statement that I have come across in five years.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Just force of habit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, at page 10 of that statement, the second paragraph. You have that in front of you that you can read it, sir? You said this: "At about 1300 hours, I together with Sergeant Major Rave, returned to Bratunac to solve the issue of fuel for buses with the Serbs." Now, is that what you said during your second statement?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, I'll ask you this. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You then went on to say you spoke to Major Nikolic. "He informed me that buses were on the way and that we had better find fuel for them." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If that's how it reads, then that's how it reads.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now -- I'll ask you this. Was there an agreement between the DutchBat and General Mladic that DutchBat would supply diesel fuel for the evacuation? Was there that agreement?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the request came from General Mladic, but I don't know whether such an agreement was made.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So that again if there were evidence to the effect that the agreement was that DutchBat and Mladic -- that the UN would supply diesel fuel for the evacuation, you wouldn't necessarily agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He already answered the question. He said he doesn't know whether such agreement -- and 100 other persons might assert that, but he's not a position to confirm or deny it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: When you returned from Bratunac to Potocari -- you said that you made observations in relation to buses and trucks heading back towards Potocari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you yourself were part physically of that first convoy out of Potocari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: This was a journey that went on for -- how long did it take you to get from Potocari to the ultimate destination? How many hours?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "final destination"?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: What is your estimation of how many kilometres you travelled from Potocari to the point where you concluded -- where the refugees were taken off the buses at the final point? How many kilometres was that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps 50 or 80 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. And so you would agree with 10 buses, I think your evidence was, and 6 trucks, a considerable amount of fuel would have been required at least for that journey. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on how you define a considerable amount.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's true. Are you able to give any evidence at all as to where the fuel came from for that first convoy?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't state anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, you simply have no idea where the fuel came from; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was already in the vehicles. I didn't see any filling up.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, your evidence in relation to the question of separation on the afternoon of the 12th of July is that men were taken to the so-called White House; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And your evidence is quite clearly that there is no dispute in your mind that you entered into this house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I entered the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You were quite specific this morning, were you not? You said that you went to the -- a room on the first floor of the house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I entered, the first area upon entering.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. And you have a specific recollection, do you not, of seeing passports and identity cards in that room that you entered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember seeing them in a corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, you were shown a photo this morning of the so-called White House. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You would agree that there is nothing from the photograph of the White House which shows that it is a house under construction? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: This is at -- in your first statement. That's 1D00017 at page 8. I want you to have a look at the fourth paragraph, please. Sorry, the first statement, not the second statement. And page 8. The paragraph begins: "About 10 minutes later I went back outside, and I saw that the people were already being loaded onto the buses. I saw that men were being picked out by the Bosnian Serb soldiers and assembled at a house opposite the entrance to the compound." Do you see where I'm reading from?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You then went on to say: "This house was still under construction." Is that right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: "I wanted to talk over to the men but were restrained by soldiers with dogs, who told me I was not allowed to go any further." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's correct, that you went to go into the house but you were restrained? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was inside first, and afterwards I had to leave and was not allowed to re-enter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Well, you also provided a debriefing document about this question -- sorry -- about you entering that house or not. This is -- this isn't in my list, Your Honour, of exhibits but the ERN number is R0138887 at page 8, where you said this: "He further stated," this is you, "that he noticed that people were separated before entering the buses and that men were taken to the renowned house and that Major de Haan counted the people who went in and those who came out." Is that right? That's what you said in your debriefing, one of your debriefings? I should give the date. The 12th of September, 1995, it looks like.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And then you went on to say: "The witness himself could not get permission from the Serb on duty to inspect the house." Is that right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but at first I entered and was told to leave and the second time I was not allowed to go back in. So first I was inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But you agree that both in your first statement and in your debriefing you have made it very clear that you were prevented from entering the house?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I object to that characterisation. I'm sorry, I didn't wait to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Objection sustained. He never said that. There's nothing in the document from where you were reading that says that he stated that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to the question of separation itself, Colonel Boering, your evidence is that you observed separations to be occurring while General Mladic was present at Potocari; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the refugees were being transported in the buses, that was at that point men were being separated, and General Mladic was present there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And your evidence is that as I understand it you have a specific recollection of reporting the fact of separation to lieutenant Colonel Karremans; is that right? If I'm wrong, that's fine, but I just want to clarify this. And I'll ask it in a much clearer way. But did you in fact report the separations you say you saw to Lieutenant Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported this to Major Franken when I exited what was known as the White House after my first visit there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And are you able to give me an indication of what time in the afternoon that was on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think it was around 1.30 or 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: 1.30 or 2.00 that you made that report to Deputy Commander Franken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 1.30 or 2.00 or 2.30 around that time. Just before the convoy departed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That was my next question. You were part of the first convoy. What time did you leave Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a difficult question. I think it was about 3.00 or 3.30. I really don't remember exactly what time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. And what you also say is that upon arrival at Luka there were separations that you saw then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Condon. So who is going to go next tomorrow -- on Monday? It will be Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And you still anticipate an hour and fifteen minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's what I anticipate, depending on whether the witness actually listens to all the translations in Dutch before he answers. I notice he answered some of your questions straight away and other times he doesn't, so I'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. So, Colonel, we are going to stop here for this week. We will resume again on Monday. We're still in the morning on Monday, aren't we? We're still in the morning. Hopefully by Tuesday we'll try to make an effort to conclude with your testimony here. Yes. Thank you, and a nice weekend to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 25th day of September, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
